newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African budget vows action on goods smuggling.
newsitem.headline: S.African budget vows action on goods smuggling.

text.p: South Africa's 1997/98 budget makes specific provisions to try and halt the rapid increase in the smuggling of goods into the country, often undermining local industry.

The budget review released along with Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's budget speech said that ad valorem duties on certain items which were once regarded as luxuries but which had become general household products were too high.
This had created a strong incentive to smuggle these goods into the country and the present duties of 37.5 percent would be reduced to 15 percent.
These goods range from perfumes to photographic film, video recorders, cameras, watches and clothing.
Duties for motor cycles would also be cut to varying levels depending on cylinder capacity.
Manuel told reporters that he was sure that many manufacturers would welcome these cuts as they were "being run into the ground by smuggling".
The cuts would reduce the cost of importing and make smuggling less lucrative, he said.
The budget review said this would complement steps being taken to strengthen the administration of customs and excise regulations.
These included the involvement of the private sector and technical assistance from British customs officials.

"It is the intention to introduce new measures which will curb the underdeclaration of the value of goods and to reconcile the values declared for customs with that declared for foreign exchange purposes," the review said.
Extra investigation staff would be appointed this year, training would be increased and border posts would be more strictly controlled.
"These efforts, together with the reduction of rates of duties on goods which are frequently smuggled, should result in a substantial reduction in smuggling," the review said.
